extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in mathematics; aspiring mathematicians
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for doing mathematical research effectively: how to allocate effort, learn the field, manage projects, and convert intuition into rigorous work. Aimed at those training for or practicing mathematical research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work hard / sustained effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Relying on intelligence alone to pull things off at the last minute may work for a while, but, generally speaking, at the graduate level or higher it doesn’t. One needs to do a serious amount of reading and writing, and not just thinking, in order to get anywhere serious in mathematics; ... mathematical breakthroughs are ... largely a product of hard work, directed of course by experience and intuition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate sustained, directed effort rather than expecting intermittent 'Eureka' moments to carry you. Hard work includes substantial reading and writing as part of the research process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read the relevant literature and write to back up understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: If you think you understand a piece of mathematics, you should be able to back that up by having read all the relevant literature and having written down at least a sketch of how that piece of mathematics goes, and then ultimately writing up a complete and detailed treatment of the topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on informal intuition; document sketches and produce full write-ups showing you can reproduce and explain the details. Reading prior work thoroughly is part of validating understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide substantial detail / proof-of-concept before expecting others to develop idea
rubrics_metrics.description: It is only worth paying one’s time and attention to papers in which a substantial amount of detail and other supporting evidence (or at least a 'proof-of-concept') has already been carefully gathered to support one’s 'grand idea'. If the originator of the idea is unwilling to do this, chances are that no-one else will do so either.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing new ideas, include detailed supporting work or proof-of-concept; otherwise the idea will likely not be pursued by others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn and relearn your field; know tools' strengths and weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: To get to the 'post-rigorous' stage ... one has to first invest real effort in learning and relearning the field, learning the strengths and weaknesses of tools, learning what else is going on in mathematics, learning how to solve problems rigorously, and answering lots of dumb questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continually refresh and deepen your knowledge. Be explicit about what tools can and cannot do; cross-train in related areas to broaden perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct effort fruitfully; think ahead and prioritize
rubrics_metrics.description: It is also important to direct your effort in a fruitful direction rather than a fruitless one; in particular, spend some time thinking ahead, and don’t obsess on a single 'big problem' or 'big theory'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularly evaluate whether the problems you work on are likely to yield progress; plan a forward strategy and avoid becoming fixated on a single long-shot goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have multiple projects and use smaller tasks strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: I find that it helps to have a number of smaller projects (or perhaps some non-mathematical errands) to have at hand when I am unwilling for whatever reason to work on my major projects; conversely, if I get bored with these smaller tasks, I can often convince myself to then tackle one of my bigger ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a portfolio of tasks of varying size/priority so you can switch when motivation fluctuates. Small projects can sustain momentum and serve as breaks from major efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be flexible: modify goals or shelve projects when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: There are also times when one realises that a project is simply too much to handle at the present time, and it then makes sense to modify one's goals for the project, or shelve it and work on another project instead: see 'be flexible' and 'use the wastebasket'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when to change scope or pause work rather than stubbornly persisting on an intractable plan; strategic shelving can be productive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enjoy your work to sustain effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Of course, to work hard, it really helps if you enjoy your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate intrinsic enjoyment or find aspects of work you like; enjoyment supports sustained, high-quality effort over the long term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish working hard from maximizing hours; avoid counterproductive forcing
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an important distinction between 'working hard' and 'maximising the number of hours during which one works'. Forcing oneself to work even when one is tired, unmotivated, unprepared, or distracted with other tasks can end up being counterproductive ... there is a saturation point beyond which pushing oneself to work even longer will actually reduce the total amount of work you get done in the long run.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate long hours with productivity. Watch for fatigue, lack of motivation, poor preparation, or distraction as signals that extra hours will be low-yield or harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize a few hours of high-quality work when conditions are right
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally speaking, it is better to try to arrange a few hours of high-quality working time, when one is motivated, energetic, prepared, and free from distraction, than to try to cram into one’s schedule a large number of hours of low-quality working time when one or more of the above four factors are not present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optimize for work sessions where the four factors (motivated, energetic, prepared, free from distraction) are present. Plan schedules to capture those windows rather than accumulating low-quality time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept normal fluctuations in motivation and rest when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: There will of course be times when one is too frustrated, fatigued, or otherwise not motivated to work on one’s current project. This is perfectly normal, and trying to force oneself to keep at that project can become counterproductive after a while.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat lapses in motivation as normal. Use rest, alternate projects, or lower-stakes tasks rather than forcing ineffective work.
